what_this_is: The ONE statement catalogue. Before it, the LSQB battery existed three times — crates/engram-bench/src/bin/lsqb.rs (Cypher), a PostgreSQL runner script (SQL) and an embedded LadybugDB runner (Kuzu/LadybugDB Cypher) — and the stress workload existed once, in Cypher, which is why concurrency was measured on two engines and the join battery on four. Statement TEXT lives here, per dialect; the SEQUENCE, the parameters and the mix live in an emitted plan (see docs/converged-harness.md). A backend renders text from here and binds the plan's parameters; it never invents either.

provenance.lsqb.cypher: Transcribed from crates/engram-bench/src/bin/lsqb.rs, QUERIES table, string continuations resolved. That table is GONE: lsqb.rs renders from here. The bytes are locked to the ones the pre-cutover binary sent by tests/golden/lsqb-cypher-statements.txt, checked by tests/a_lsqb_statement_lives_once_and_matches_the_baseline.rs.
provenance.lsqb.sql: the PostgreSQL LSQB runner script, the q1..q9 FROM bodies, verbatim.
provenance.lsqb.cypher_ladybug: the embedded LadybugDB runner's QUERIES, verbatim (Message -> Post:Comment, NOT (a)-[:T]-(b) -> NOT EXISTS { MATCH ... }).
provenance.stress.cypher: crates/engram-bench/src/bin/stress.rs render_read/render_write/render_algo/render_churn_*, extracted from their rendered output and locked by tests/golden/stress-op-sequence.txt.

status_values.verified: this text has been executed against the engine it names and its answer checked against another engine's
status_values.unverified: transcribed from the schema and the Cypher, never executed. A run that uses it is a first run, not a comparison.
status_values.unsupported: this dialect cannot express the shape; `reason` says why. Declared, never dropped — the lsqb `unmappable` discipline.

cypher_ladybug.rel_alternation_note: LadybugDB/Kuzu store one rel table per (type, src-table, dst-table) pair, so a type spanning several pairs must be written as the alternation of its pair tables. The executor substitutes `[:TYPE]` -> `[:TYPE_Src_Dst|TYPE_Src2_Dst2]` from the pairs.json its own loader wrote. That substitution is a property of the LOADED corpus, not of this catalogue, which is why it is declared here and applied there.

lsqb.corpus_note: Counts are properties of WHATEVER corpus is loaded — snbgen synthetic or converted official Datagen. They are comparable across engines loading the SAME corpus and never against published LSQB results.
lsqb.expected_note: `sf1` and `sf3` are the official Datagen scale factors as loaded on the bench pod. An entry that is absent carries NO expectation; it is not an expectation of zero.

cypher.text: MATCH (:Country)<-[:IS_PART_OF]-(:City)<-[:IS_LOCATED_IN]-(:Person)<-[:HAS_MEMBER]-(:Forum)-[:CONTAINER_OF]->(:Post)<-[:REPLY_OF]-(:Comment)-[:HAS_TAG]->(:Tag)-[:HAS_TYPE]->(:TagClass) RETURN count(*) AS count

sql.body: FROM IS_PART_OF_City_Country cpc JOIN IS_LOCATED_IN_Person_City plc ON plc.dst = cpc.src JOIN HAS_MEMBER_Forum_Person fhm ON fhm.dst = plc.src JOIN CONTAINER_OF_Forum_Post fcp ON fcp.src = fhm.src JOIN REPLY_OF_Comment_Post crp ON crp.dst = fcp.dst JOIN HAS_TAG_Comment_Tag cht ON cht.src = crp.src JOIN HAS_TYPE_Tag_TagClass tht ON tht.src = cht.dst

cypher.text: MATCH (person1:Person)-[:KNOWS]-(person2:Person), (person1)<-[:HAS_CREATOR]-(comment:Comment)-[:REPLY_OF]->(post:Post)-[:HAS_CREATOR]->(person2) RETURN count(*) AS count

sql.body: FROM knows_sym k JOIN HAS_CREATOR_Comment_Person chc ON chc.dst = k.src JOIN REPLY_OF_Comment_Post crp ON crp.src = chc.src JOIN HAS_CREATOR_Post_Person phc ON phc.src = crp.dst AND phc.dst = k.dst

cypher.text: MATCH (country:Country) MATCH (person1:Person)-[:IS_LOCATED_IN]->(city1:City)-[:IS_PART_OF]->(country) MATCH (person2:Person)-[:IS_LOCATED_IN]->(city2:City)-[:IS_PART_OF]->(country) MATCH (person3:Person)-[:IS_LOCATED_IN]->(city3:City)-[:IS_PART_OF]->(country) MATCH (person1)-[:KNOWS]-(person2)-[:KNOWS]-(person3)-[:KNOWS]-(person1) RETURN count(*) AS count

cypher_ladybug.text: MATCH (country:Country) MATCH (person1:Person)-[:IS_LOCATED_IN]->(city1:City)-[:IS_PART_OF]->(country) MATCH (person2:Person)-[:IS_LOCATED_IN]->(city2:City)-[:IS_PART_OF]->(country) MATCH (person3:Person)-[:IS_LOCATED_IN]->(city3:City)-[:IS_PART_OF]->(country) MATCH (person1)-[:KNOWS]-(person2)-[:KNOWS]-(person3)-[:KNOWS]-(person1) RETURN count(*) AS count

sql.body: FROM IS_LOCATED_IN_Person_City p1 JOIN IS_PART_OF_City_Country c1 ON c1.src = p1.dst JOIN IS_LOCATED_IN_Person_City p2 ON true JOIN IS_PART_OF_City_Country c2 ON c2.src = p2.dst AND c2.dst = c1.dst JOIN IS_LOCATED_IN_Person_City p3 ON true JOIN IS_PART_OF_City_Country c3 ON c3.src = p3.dst AND c3.dst = c1.dst JOIN knows_sym k12 ON k12.src = p1.src AND k12.dst = p2.src JOIN knows_sym k23 ON k23.src = p2.src AND k23.dst = p3.src JOIN knows_sym k31 ON k31.src = p3.src AND k31.dst = p1.src

cypher.text: MATCH (:Tag)<-[:HAS_TAG]-(message:Message)-[:HAS_CREATOR]->(creator:Person), (message)<-[:LIKES]-(liker:Person), (message)<-[:REPLY_OF]-(comment:Comment) RETURN count(*) AS count

sql.body: FROM Message_hasTag_Tag mht JOIN Message_hasCreator_Person mhc ON mhc.src = mht.src JOIN Person_likes_Message plm ON plm.dst = mht.src JOIN Comment_replyOf_Message crm ON crm.dst = mht.src

cypher.text: MATCH (tag1:Tag)<-[:HAS_TAG]-(message:Message)<-[:REPLY_OF]-(comment:Comment)-[:HAS_TAG]->(tag2:Tag) WHERE tag1 <> tag2 RETURN count(*) AS count

cypher_ladybug.text: MATCH (tag1:Tag)<-[:HAS_TAG]-(message:Post:Comment)<-[:REPLY_OF]-(comment:Comment)-[:HAS_TAG]->(tag2:Tag) WHERE tag1 <> tag2 RETURN count(*) AS count

sql.body: FROM Message_hasTag_Tag mt1 JOIN Comment_replyOf_Message crm ON crm.dst = mt1.src JOIN HAS_TAG_Comment_Tag ct2 ON ct2.src = crm.src WHERE mt1.dst <> ct2.dst

cypher.text: MATCH (person1:Person)-[:KNOWS]-(person2:Person)-[:KNOWS]-(person3:Person)-[:HAS_INTEREST]->(tag:Tag) WHERE person1 <> person3 RETURN count(*) AS count

cypher_ladybug.text: MATCH (person1:Person)-[:KNOWS]-(person2:Person)-[:KNOWS]-(person3:Person)-[:HAS_INTEREST]->(tag:Tag) WHERE person1 <> person3 RETURN count(*) AS count

sql.body: FROM knows_sym k1 JOIN knows_sym k2 ON k2.src = k1.dst JOIN HAS_INTEREST_Person_Tag pit ON pit.src = k2.dst WHERE k1.src <> k2.dst

cypher.text: MATCH (:Tag)<-[:HAS_TAG]-(message:Message)-[:HAS_CREATOR]->(creator:Person) OPTIONAL MATCH (message)<-[:LIKES]-(liker:Person) OPTIONAL MATCH (message)<-[:REPLY_OF]-(comment:Comment) RETURN count(*) AS count

cypher_ladybug.text: MATCH (:Tag)<-[:HAS_TAG]-(message:Post:Comment)-[:HAS_CREATOR]->(creator:Person) OPTIONAL MATCH (message)<-[:LIKES]-(liker:Person) OPTIONAL MATCH (message)<-[:REPLY_OF]-(comment:Comment) RETURN count(*) AS count

sql.body: FROM Message_hasTag_Tag mht JOIN Message_hasCreator_Person mhc ON mhc.src = mht.src LEFT JOIN Person_likes_Message plm ON plm.dst = mht.src LEFT JOIN Comment_replyOf_Message crm ON crm.dst = mht.src

cypher.text: MATCH (tag1:Tag)<-[:HAS_TAG]-(message:Message)<-[:REPLY_OF]-(comment:Comment)-[:HAS_TAG]->(tag2:Tag) WHERE NOT (comment)-[:HAS_TAG]->(tag1) AND tag1 <> tag2 RETURN count(*) AS count

cypher_ladybug.text: MATCH (tag1:Tag)<-[:HAS_TAG]-(message:Post:Comment)<-[:REPLY_OF]-(comment:Comment)-[:HAS_TAG]->(tag2:Tag) WHERE NOT EXISTS { MATCH (comment)-[:HAS_TAG]->(tag1) } AND tag1 <> tag2 RETURN count(*) AS count

sql.body: FROM Message_hasTag_Tag mt1 JOIN Comment_replyOf_Message crm ON crm.dst = mt1.src JOIN HAS_TAG_Comment_Tag ct2 ON ct2.src = crm.src WHERE mt1.dst <> ct2.dst AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM HAS_TAG_Comment_Tag x WHERE x.src = crm.src AND x.dst = mt1.dst)

cypher.text: MATCH (person1:Person)-[:KNOWS]-(person2:Person)-[:KNOWS]-(person3:Person)-[:HAS_INTEREST]->(tag:Tag) WHERE NOT (person1)-[:KNOWS]-(person3) AND person1 <> person3 RETURN count(*) AS count

cypher_ladybug.text: MATCH (person1:Person)-[:KNOWS]-(person2:Person)-[:KNOWS]-(person3:Person)-[:HAS_INTEREST]->(tag:Tag) WHERE NOT EXISTS { MATCH (person1)-[:KNOWS]-(person3) } AND person1 <> person3 RETURN count(*) AS count

sql.body: FROM knows_sym k1 JOIN knows_sym k2 ON k2.src = k1.dst JOIN HAS_INTEREST_Person_Tag pit ON pit.src = k2.dst WHERE k1.src <> k2.dst AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM knows_sym x WHERE x.src = k1.src AND x.dst = k2.dst)

sql_shape.note: pg-lsqb.sh's protocol, kept: the probe is the SAME body with the aggregate replaced, so an anti-join's zero is proven with the NOT applied. The Cypher dialects derive their probe the same way, by replacing the `RETURN count(*) AS count` suffix with `RETURN 1 LIMIT 1`.

table_alias.note: The SQL schema materialises the Message supertype and a symmetric KNOWS, so a table name does not equal a relationship type. This map is what the catalogue-equivalence test uses to compare the SQL's joined tables against the Cypher's relationship types.

lsqb.skeleton_note: is the multiset of relationship-type traversals the query performs, ANTI-JOIN legs included: q8 walks HAS_TAG three times (twice in the pattern, once inside the NOT) and the SQL joins HAS_TAG_Comment_Tag three times for the same reason. Counting only the joined legs would let a dialect drop an anti-join and still match.

census._note: An empty corpus answers 0 to every query and would pass vacuously, so a run against one fails before measuring anything. Two statements, not one: a corpus with nodes but no :Person is a corpus loaded from the wrong export, and the whole battery would then answer 0 legitimately.

cypher_ladybug.note: LadybugDB has no all-tables node count in one statement — a node IS its table — so the Person count stands for both. Declared rather than silently skipped: the guard is weaker on this engine, not absent.

sql.nodes: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM Person) + (SELECT count(*) FROM Tag) AS c
sql.persons: SELECT count(*) AS c FROM Person

cypher_ladybug.reason: an all-tables node count has no single-statement form; the executor sums per-table counts from its own loader manifest

census.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM stress) AS c

synthetic.what: the harness seeds its own world, so a four-engine concurrency comparison needs no corpus at all
sql_schema: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS stress (k bigint PRIMARY KEY, b int NOT NULL, pad text NOT NULL, hits bigint)
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS link (src bigint NOT NULL, dst bigint NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS slink (src bigint NOT NULL, dst bigint NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS stressw (id bigint NOT NULL, c bigint NOT NULL, s bigint NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS msgnode (id bigint, creation_date bigint, content text, length int, mid bigint, mdate bigint, mtext text, mlen int)
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS uniq (u bigint PRIMARY KEY)
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS churn_anchor (cid bigint NOT NULL, nonce bigint NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS churn (id bigint NOT NULL, cid bigint NOT NULL, nonce bigint NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS churn_rel (acid bigint NOT NULL, anonce bigint NOT NULL, id bigint NOT NULL, nonce bigint NOT NULL)
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS stress_b ON stress (b)
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS link_src ON link (src, dst)
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS link_dst ON link (dst, src)
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS churn_key ON churn (nonce, id)
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS churn_anchor_key ON churn_anchor (nonce, cid)
synthetic.sql_schema_note: BUILT by the harness, unlike snb's, and the asymmetry is the point: on Bolt the synthetic corpus needs no DDL because the graph is schemaless, so a SQL arm that did not run this would fail its first seed statement with `relation "stress" does not exist` and the dataset's promise - that it runs anywhere, including CI, with no corpus at all - would hold on three engines out of four. `IF NOT EXISTS` throughout because the harness runs the whole list on every start; without it a second run dies on the first CREATE. `stressw.id` is deliberately NOT a primary key: the Bolt arm's `CREATE (:StressW {c, s})` admits duplicates, so a PK here would make the same plan replayed twice at one level index refuse EVERY write, and a level that measured refusals would sit in the table beside levels that measured inserts. Level scoping stays checkable on this arm without it - `uniq.u` IS a primary key, and every churn survivor probe is bounded by the level's own id range, so a dropped stride shows up as total churn loss rather than as nothing.
sql_seed: INSERT INTO stress (k, b, pad) SELECT i, i % 16, 'x' FROM generate_series(${lo}, ${hi}) AS i
INSERT INTO link (src, dst) SELECT a.k, b.k FROM stress a JOIN stress b ON b.k = (a.k * 7 + 1) % ${keys} WHERE a.k >= ${lo} AND a.k <= ${hi}
synthetic.sql_seed_post_note: Run ONCE after the seeding loop, never inside a measured window. A PostgreSQL that has never been ANALYZEd plans against default selectivity guesses, so the first comparison would be against a planner working blind - and autovacuum's own first pass would otherwise land at an unpredictable point inside a level and show up as a mid-run throughput step nobody could attribute. The Cypher arm declares no equivalent because its index fixtures already force the one deferred build it has.
synthetic.sql_seed_note: The Cypher seeder writes the same two populations in 500-row UNWIND batches. The set is identical; the write PATH is not, and no engine's seed time is a measured number in this harness. These are bounded by the SAME [lo, hi] batch window as the Cypher templates because the harness has ONE seeding loop for every dialect. The first version of this entry was set-based over the whole key space and bound `${keys_minus_1}`, which nothing supplies - so the harness issued forty identical whole-population INSERTs, each still carrying the literal characters `${keys_minus_1}`, and PostgreSQL answered `syntax error at or near "$"`. Observed 2026-09-09, on the first statement PgBackend ever sent. That is why seed_or_attach now refuses a template that still carries an unbound placeholder instead of letting the engine's parser be the thing that notices.
cypher_seed: UNWIND range(${lo}, ${hi}) AS i CREATE (:Stress {k: i, b: i % 16, pad: 'x'})
UNWIND range(${lo}, ${hi}) AS i MATCH (a:Stress {k: i}), (b:Stress {k: (i * 7 + 1) % ${keys}}) CREATE (a)-[:LINK]->(b)
synthetic.cypher_seed_note: The two populations stress.rs seeds, as UNWIND batches over a [lo, hi] range so seeding is not itself the bottleneck. Batch SIZE is the harness s (500, as stress.rs uses); the SET is what matters and it is identical. No engine s seed time is a measured number in this harness.
synthetic.census_note: One census per dialect, and the SQL one is not decoration: seed_or_attach reads it to refuse a SECOND seeding pass over a corpus it already built. It used to be skipped on `sql` because only the Cypher form existed, and a skipped guard on this arm means the second run either doubles the population or - `stress.k` being a primary key - refuses every seed statement and stops. Neither is a corpus anybody chose. The guard compares against --keys, so a corpus seeded SMALLER than the run asks for is not skipped: the seed loop starts again from 0, and on SQL the first batch collides with `stress.k` and stops the run at `seed failed at 0`. That is the right answer badly worded, and it is louder than the Cypher arm's, which has no primary key and simply grows a second overlapping population. Point a differently sized run at a fresh database rather than growing one in place.

snb.what: ATTACH to a server that already holds an LDBC SNB corpus; --keys is probed from it
snb.sql_schema_status: BUILT 2026-09-09. docs/bench/pg-snb-load.sh loaded it into `sf1` and `sf3` on the PostgreSQL benchmark server from /datasets/jsonl/sf{1,3}, and docs/bench/pg-snb-verify.sql checked every table against the corpus manifest AND against the tables pg-lsqb.sh loaded from the split-CSV export. Every `snb` SQL entry nevertheless stays `unverified`: each has now been EXECUTED and returns plausible rows, but no answer has been compared with engram's, and `verified` in this catalogue means cross-checked.
snb.sql_schema_note: pg-lsqb.sh's relational shape carries ids ONLY (`CREATE TABLE Person (id bigint PRIMARY KEY)`) because LSQB counts subgraphs and never reads a property. Every SNB stress read shape reads properties — firstName, birthday, browserUsed, Tag.name, City.name. This list is the shape that adds them. It is owned by the CORPUS LOADER, not by the harness: seed_or_attach runs `sql_schema` only on the seeding branch, and `snb` attaches, so nothing here is ever executed by a run. docs/bench/pg-snb-schema.sql is the implementation and tests/a_sql_statement_names_only_tables_and_columns_its_schema_declares.rs is what holds the two together — it was that test, not a reading, that found the five `any`-family tables missing below.

CREATE TABLE reply_of (src bigint NOT NULL, dst bigint NOT NULL)

snb.sql_any_family_note: The last five tables — msgnode, uniq, churn_anchor, churn, churn_rel — were absent from this list until 2026-09-09 and belong here because the write ops that use them (node_only, node_only_fresh_props, unique_create, churn_anchor, churn_create, churn_delete) are declared `any`, meaning they render the SAME text on every corpus. They appear under `synthetic` as well, and the duplication is deliberate: a dataset's sql_schema must be the WHOLE schema a run on that dataset needs, or the check that compares statements against it can only be as complete as the list.
snb.sql_index_note: One index per access path an SNB statement actually takes, and no others, because both errors are fatal to a comparison and only one of them looks wrong. Three indexes this list used to carry are gone. `person_name (first_name, last_name)` served only the plat-composite shapes, which are `unsupported` in SQL, and the Cypher fixture group for `snb` does not build a name index either — only `snb-platform` does — so it would have given Postgres a structure engram does not carry. `knows_dst` has no reader: `knows` is stored symmetrically, so the mirror row IS the reverse lookup, and every statement probes it by src. `has_creator_src` has no reader either AND has_creator is written on every node_create, so it was a per-write tax with nothing on the other side. Three are new and matter more: has_tag_src (ic6-friend-tags probes by src), reply_of_dst (is7-replies probes by dst) and churn_rel_key (churn_delete deletes by (nonce, id) on every second churn op, against a table that grows all run). Without those three the statements are sequential scans of multi-million-row tables per operation — not a slower Postgres, a rigged one. Verified by EXPLAIN against sf1 on 2026-09-09: with churn_rel_key dropped the delete plans as `Seq Scan on churn_rel`, and with it as `Index Scan using churn_rel_key`. `is_located_in` is deliberately UNINDEXED: its only reader, agg-by-city, aggregates the whole table.
snb.sql_planner_note: NOT a schema problem, recorded here because it will show up as one. With a non-zero max_parallel_workers_per_gather — which PgBackend::connect sets from --thread-cap — the ic6-friend-tags plan costs a parallel aggregate at 28,280 against a serial 34,957 and therefore chooses it, which forces `Parallel Seq Scan on knows` (cost 4,609) in place of `Index Only Scan using knows_src` (cost 50), because a scan under Gather must be parallel-aware. Measured by EXPLAIN against sf1 on 2026-09-09; at max_parallel_workers_per_gather=0 the index is used immediately. It is one shape of nine at weight 5, and Postgres spending the thread budget INSIDE a query where engram spends it across clients is arguably the honest reading of a thread cap. What is not honest is leaving it unsaid: the PostgreSQL benchmark server capped max_parallel_workers at 6 CLUSTER-WIDE, so at 32 clients most Gather nodes find no worker and run the parallel plan in the leader alone — still scanning the whole knows table, now with nothing parallel about it. --thread-cap 0 fixes the plan and also changes the fairness block, which the reporter compares for equality, so it is a decision about both arms rather than an adjustment to one.
snb.knows_note: `knows` must be SYMMETRIC (both directions stored), as pg-lsqb.sh's `knows_sym` is, because every `-[:KNOWS]-` in the Cypher is undirected.
snb.cypher_attach_note: ATTACH, not seed: the corpus is already there and --keys is PROBED from it rather than trusted. A key space larger than the corpus makes most lookups miss, and a run whose reads mostly return nothing measures the index s negative path and reports it as throughput. The probe returns one ROW per person rather than a count(*) scalar because the row count IS the answer and snbgen emits dense ids 0..persons.

snb-platform.what: the SNB corpus read through the platform's own access shapes
snb-platform.cross_engine_reason: these seven shapes exist to reproduce ONE production system's access paths on engram against Neo4j, over Bolt. Transcribing them to SQL would produce a comparison nobody asked for and would change what `--dataset snb-platform` means. Declared out of scope rather than half-mapped.

cypher.text: MATCH (n:Stress {k: ${key}}) RETURN n.k, n.pad

sql.text: SELECT k, pad FROM stress WHERE k = ${key}

cypher.text: MATCH (n:Stress {k: ${key}})-[:LINK]->(m) RETURN m.k LIMIT 25

sql.text: SELECT m.k FROM link l JOIN stress m ON m.k = l.dst WHERE l.src = ${key} LIMIT 25

cypher.text: MATCH (n:Stress {k: ${key}})-[:LINK]->()-[:LINK]->(m) RETURN m.k LIMIT 25

sql.text: SELECT m.k FROM link l1 JOIN link l2 ON l2.src = l1.dst JOIN stress m ON m.k = l2.dst WHERE l1.src = ${key} LIMIT 25

cypher.text: MATCH (n:Stress {k: ${key}})-[:LINK*1..2]->(m) RETURN count(m) AS c

sql.text: SELECT count(*) AS c FROM (SELECT l.dst FROM link l WHERE l.src = ${key} UNION ALL SELECT l2.dst FROM link l1 JOIN link l2 ON l2.src = l1.dst AND (l2.src, l2.dst) <> (l1.src, l1.dst) WHERE l1.src = ${key}) t
sql.note: The `(l2.src, l2.dst) <> (l1.src, l1.dst)` term is Cypher's relationship-uniqueness rule within one path, written out. `link` carries no edge id, so the pair stands in for one; that is exact here because the seeder writes each (src, dst) once.

cypher.text: MATCH (n:Stress) WHERE n.b = ${b} RETURN n.b, count(*) AS c

cypher_ladybug.text: MATCH (n:Stress) WHERE n.b = ${b} RETURN n.b, count(*) AS c

sql.text: SELECT b, count(*) AS c FROM stress WHERE b = ${b} GROUP BY b

cypher.text: MATCH (n:Stress) RETURN n.k ORDER BY n.k DESC LIMIT 20

cypher_ladybug.text: MATCH (n:Stress) RETURN n.k ORDER BY n.k DESC LIMIT 20

sql.text: SELECT k FROM stress ORDER BY k DESC LIMIT 20

cypher.text: MATCH (n:Stress) WHERE n.k > ${key} RETURN count(n) AS c

cypher_ladybug.text: MATCH (n:Stress) WHERE n.k > ${key} RETURN count(n) AS c

sql.text: SELECT count(*) AS c FROM stress WHERE k > ${key}

cypher.text: MATCH (p:Person {id: ${key}}) RETURN p.firstName, p.lastName, p.birthday, p.locationIP, p.browserUsed

cypher_ladybug.text: MATCH (p:Person {id: ${key}}) RETURN p.firstName, p.lastName, p.birthday, p.locationIP, p.browserUsed

sql.text: SELECT first_name, last_name, birthday, location_ip, browser_used FROM person WHERE id = ${key}

cypher.text: MATCH (p:Person {id: ${key}})-[:KNOWS]-(f:Person) RETURN f.id, f.firstName LIMIT 25

sql.text: SELECT f.id, f.first_name FROM knows k JOIN person f ON f.id = k.dst WHERE k.src = ${key} LIMIT 25

cypher.text: MATCH (p:Person {id: ${key}})-[:KNOWS]-()-[:KNOWS]-(f:Person) RETURN count(DISTINCT f) AS c

cypher_ladybug.text: MATCH (p:Person {id: ${key}})-[:KNOWS]-(:Person)-[:KNOWS]-(f:Person) RETURN count(DISTINCT f) AS c

sql.text: SELECT count(DISTINCT k2.dst) AS c FROM knows k1 JOIN knows k2 ON k2.src = k1.dst AND (k2.src, k2.dst) <> (k1.dst, k1.src) WHERE k1.src = ${key}

cypher.text: MATCH (m:Message)-[:HAS_CREATOR]->(p:Person {id: ${key}}) RETURN m.id LIMIT 25

sql.text: SELECT m.id FROM has_creator hc JOIN message m ON m.id = hc.src WHERE hc.dst = ${key} LIMIT 25

delete-churn._note: The per-level clean slate, and the ANCHOR half of it is load-bearing. Anchors carry no level identity, so a level that left the previous level s anchors in place would find TWO ChurnAnchor rows for (cid, nonce): the create MATCHes both and one acked statement mints two nodes. Measured here on 2026-09-09 before the sweep deleted them - level 1 reported 100 survivors against an expected 67 and 33 duplicate ids, which is exactly level 0 s survivor count. Deleting this run s anchors orphans the previous level s survivors (they keep their node, lose their rel); that is harmless because every anchor-rel check is bounded to the level s own id range. The Churn delete is bounded by the id RANGE rather than by the nonce, because under a plan one nonce covers the whole sweep.

setup: CREATE INDEX churn_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:Churn) ON (n.id)
CREATE INDEX churn_anchor_cid IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:ChurnAnchor) ON (n.cid)
MATCH (n:Churn) WHERE n.nonce = ${nonce} AND n.id >= ${lo} AND n.id < ${hi} DETACH DELETE n
MATCH (a:ChurnAnchor) WHERE a.nonce = ${nonce} DETACH DELETE a
DELETE FROM churn_rel WHERE nonce = ${nonce} AND id >= ${lo} AND id < ${hi}
DELETE FROM churn WHERE nonce = ${nonce} AND id >= ${lo} AND id < ${hi}
sql.note: The third statement is the DETACH half of the fourth. Cypher's `DETACH DELETE a` takes every CHURN rel hanging off the anchor with it; a relational DELETE takes the anchor row alone and leaves the edge rows behind, because `churn_rel` carries no foreign key. What the leftovers do depends on the sweep, which is why this was nearly missed: an ASCENDING sweep re-creates an anchor with the same (cid, nonce) at the next level, so the orphans silently re-bind and every probe passes. A sweep whose next level has FEWER clients does not re-create the higher cids, and the orphans then bind nothing. Measured 2026-09-09 against PostgreSQL 17.11 with this statement removed: `delete-churn 2,1` reported `48 CHURN edge(s) but only 32 bind both endpoints - DANGLING EDGES` at the second level and failed the run; with it, the same sweep passes. A probe that cries wolf on a workload that did nothing wrong is worse than no probe, because it teaches the reader to discount the one time it is right.
